explanation: Fires in code on tokens inside loop headers, array sizes and range expressions that come right before a numeric bound or length, e.g. ' i' or ' <' in 'for (i=0; i<len', ' range' in 'for i in range(', '[' in 'char x[16]', ',' in 'range(0,2)'. Weak outside code; prose number ranges and math give only weak-to-moderate activation.

Fires on ordinary content words in running English prose, mostly verbs, participles and modifiers in the middle of a clause (' captured', ' visit', ' built', ' married', ' geographic', ' birthday'). No clear lexical or contextual trigger I can find; it looks like a generic mid-sentence word detector, weaker in code and boilerplate.

Fires on a token that is the predictable continuation of a fixed phrase or word: 'how' after 'no matter' / 'doesn't matter', 'since' in 'changed since', 'a' after 'absence of', 'cul' before 'minate', '-c' in 'stress-coping'/'shock-corded', 'ser' in 'serpentine'. Strongest for 'no matter how'; other tokens are idiom or word-piece continuations.

Fires on the function word or space that introduces a quantity or measure qualifier: 'in' in '15 feet in diameter' / 'in the US', 'at' in 'at its narrowest' / 'at the time', 'no'/'not' in 'essentially no more' / 'at least not', the space before the day in 'December 31'/'January 23', 'height:'. The context is usually a measurement, statistic or date.

Fires on highly predictable tokens inside formulaic templates: ' of' in the license boilerplate 'obtain a copy of the License', '[' in PHP '$_POST['', '="' in '<meta name="', 'KEY' in 'HKEY', 'relates to' in patent text, '{' in '\usepackage{', plus completions of technical words ('zo' in tetrachlorodibenzo, 'ugh' in Child-Pugh). It responds to near-certain continuations in boilerplate code and text.

Fires on a token that completes a word or set phrase whose ending is strongly predictable from what came before: 'ag' in 'coagulation', 'way' in 'all the way', 'life' in 'come to life', 'ered' in 'checkered flag', 'techn' in 'Polytechnic', 'such' in 'groups such as'. Strongest on 'co[ag]ulation'.

Fires on a 't'/'T' letter token, usually word-initial in a word split into pieces ('T'+'asting', 'T'+'ucson', Cyrillic 'т', Greek 'τ', Turkish/Spanish 't'), and on 'ot' pieces inside medical words ('normotensive', 'genotyped', 'orthotopic', 'haplotypes'). It responds to the token's spelling (the t sound) more than to its meaning.

Fires on tokens in technical, scientific or patent prose, mostly word pieces that continue a compound or specialist term ('rim' in pyrimidine, '-shaped', '-w' in spirally-wound, 'ucing' in apoptosis-inducing, 'hum' in dehumidifier, 'medial', 'micro'), and on list commas in such text. The context is dense biomedical or engineering description.

Fires on tokens inside identifiers, numbers or codes that continue an earlier pattern: a digit or letter inside a price, ID, date or barcode ('$3[5].95', '201[9]', '25002'), '*s' or '*p' variable terms in algebra, '_Profile' or 'resource' in foreign-key names, '/' in dates and URLs. It also catches a few prose words like 'theirs' and 'share'.

Fires on a punctuation-symbol token that begins a special name in prose: the '.' in '.NET', '.doc', '.php', '.data()', '.woocommerce', and '-', '#', '/', '*', ':', '%' when they start a prefix, CSS selector, subreddit or code token ('-webkit-', ':visited', '/r/', '#3'). It needs a space before the symbol and a name right after it.

Fires on the token ' out' (or 'Out'), both as a separate word ('out there', 'out of', 'out and about') and as a prefix ('outsource', 'outages', 'outpatients', 'outplayed'). Related words for exterior or foreign ('exterior', 'external', 'foreign', 'outside', 'salir') get moderate activation.

Fires on tokens that complete a predictable phrase or construction, in very different settings: 'Regards,\n' before a sign-off name, 'TERMINATED' in 'FIELDS TERMINATED BY', 'Coder' in initWithCoder, 'into' in 'blend into', 'quality' in 'mate quality', 'sealed' in 'vacuum sealed'. I see no shared topic or token.

Mixture: action verbs right after a character subject in narrative prose ('he came back', 'the coyote steps back', 'Dillard slowed'), sentence-initial 'She'/'her' in dialogue or stories, and digits in timestamps and voltages ('06:5[9].898', ' 3.3 V'). The narrative part is the most consistent.

Fires on assorted tokens with no obvious shared trait: 'file' in Apache license headers ('licenses this file', 'use this file'), the start of a new sentence or statement after a line break ('\tresult', ' Brian', 'Derek', 'Petersburg'), pronouns in dialogue, and variables in math word problems.

Fires on a mix of tokens in boilerplate and structured text: ' content' after '<meta name=...', ' *' at the start of license comment lines, ' <' before an email in author lines, '/config' in include paths, plus scattered prose words ('in series', 'me wrong', 'ahead'). I can't see one rule.

Fires on structural punctuation and operator tokens in C-like or scripting code, especially in control flow: ';' separating for-loop clauses, ')' and ' {' closing an if-condition, ' =' in assignments, '&&', ' +', and a statement keyword at a new line (' return', 'if'). Strongest inside for and if headers in JavaScript/Java/C#/Go.

Fires on function words such as articles and prepositions ('den', 'el', 'en', 'de', 'a', 'the', 'in') in mid-sentence, strongest in German, Spanish and French text. In English it fires moderately on articles in sports or news narration ('for a two-point win').

Fires on punctuation and separators next to CJK text: full-width colons, brackets and quotes (「 ： （ ， 　), '年', and ASCII delimiters ('(', '">', '/**', ' AFP') right before or after Chinese or Japanese characters. Weak on similar delimiters in non-CJK text.

Fires on assorted mid-sentence tokens in expository text that qualify or quantify ('applications to other', '4 of the 5', '15% of', 'one of', 'two- or three-', 'to name a few', 'does what it says'), plus unrelated code and word-piece tokens. Partitive and quantifier words are the most recurrent part; the rest is mixed.

Fires on the second item of a repeated or parallel structure: the second price in '$35.95 $67.95' or '£288.3 £130', the second dimension in '9.4 x 12.9', 'y' in a repeated IP pattern, the variable in 'Solve ... for v', a repeated form field label. Many examples are mixed (French XML words, license 'and').

Fires on tokens in web and HTML/programming boilerplate, especially ' charset' in '<meta ... charset=', 'meta', 'decodeURIComponent', 'UnityEditor', '.inflate', 'MustCompile'. It also fires on unrelated prose words ('outpatient', 'internationally', 'Anaheim', 'overshadowed'). The charset/meta part is consistent; the rest is mixed.
